Tuesday. In class, Sir held up Darshan's messy map and said, "This is what not to do." A few kids laughed. At home Darshan slammed the gate and shouted at Moti the dog for barking. Moti slunk under the cot.
Thursday. His older brother Madhav found him sitting on the steps. "You yelled at Moti. Moti didn't do anything. Did something happen at school?" Darshan told him about the map, his voice wobbling.
Next Monday. Darshan came home quiet, but he stroked Moti's ears first. Then he said, "Bhaiya, Sir did it again today. Can I tell you?"

qa.q: What did Sir say when he held up Darshan's map?
qa.a: "This is what not to do."

qa.q: Why did Darshan shout at Moti for barking?
qa.a: Darshan felt humiliated in class but couldn't answer back to Sir, so the feeling spilled out at home on Moti, where it felt safe.

qa.q: What turning point came from Madhav's question on Thursday?
qa.a: Madhav gently linked the yelling to school, so Darshan could say what had happened; by Monday he talked first instead of taking it out on Moti.

qa.q: How might Moti experience Darshan's homecoming on Tuesday?
qa.a: Moti gets shouted at for an ordinary bark and hides under the cot, with no idea what went wrong.

grounding: Over a week a boy humiliated by his teacher shouts at the family dog, until his brother helps him name the real hurt.

Dilnaz, jaan, you slammed three doors today. Come, sit with your Nani Zeenat. Let me tell you about a girl in Bhopal, fifty years ago.
She was eleven. Her Urdu teacher read her essay aloud to the class, mistakes and all, in a mocking voice. Everyone laughed. The girl said nothing at school. At home she banged every door in the house, and when our cat Billo rubbed against her legs, she pushed Billo away and shouted.
That girl was me. My Ammi didn't scold me. She said, "The doors didn't laugh at you, beta. Who did?" Then I cried the real tears.
So. Who laughed at you today?

qa.q: What did young Zeenat do when Billo rubbed against her legs?
qa.a: She pushed Billo away and shouted.

qa.q: Why did young Zeenat bang every door at home instead of answering the teacher?
qa.a: Answering the teacher felt impossible, so the humiliation came out at home, where it felt safe to be angry.

qa.q: What did Ammi's question 'Who did?' make possible?
qa.a: It pointed Zeenat back to the real hurt at school, so she could cry about it instead of fighting the doors and the cat.

qa.q: Why might Nani Zeenat tell this story instead of scolding Dilnaz?
qa.a: Nani seems to recognise the door-slamming from her own childhood and wants Dilnaz to name the real hurt, just as her Ammi once helped her do.

grounding: A grandmother recalls slamming doors and pushing the cat away at eleven after a teacher mocked her essay, to help her grandchild name the real hurt.

Papa had worked the night shift and was asleep behind the thin curtain, so the rule in the small flat was: no noise until four. But Gopika, nine, came in and slammed the door so hard the steel plates rattled. When Bholu the dog trotted up, she snapped, "Go away, stupid!" and he backed off.
Her father, Arnab, sat up, bleary. He could have shouted. Instead he patted the mat. "Bholu's done nothing. Something happened at school."
Gopika's chin shook. "Ma'am made me stand outside because I forgot my notebook. Everyone saw."
"That's hard." Arnab yawned. "Next time slam your pillow, not the door. And tell me first."

qa.q: Why did Ma'am make Gopika stand outside?
qa.a: Because she forgot her notebook.

qa.q: Why does Gopika snap at Bholu?
qa.a: Gopika felt humiliated when everyone saw her standing outside, and home felt safe enough to let the anger out, even at Bholu, who had done nothing.

qa.q: What choice did Arnab make when he was woken, and why did it help?
qa.a: Instead of shouting, he named that something had happened at school and gave Gopika a safer outlet, the pillow, plus a chance to tell him first 🙂

qa.q: How might Bholu see Gopika's homecoming?
qa.a: Bholu trots up happy to see her and gets called stupid, so he backs off, confused.

grounding: A nine-year-old humiliated at school slams the door and snaps at the dog in a flat where her night-shift father is sleeping.

passage:
Wasim, ten, walked home through Tolichowki with his ears still hot. In maths, Ma'am had held up his notebook. "Is this handwriting or an ant walking in ink?" The whole row had laughed, even Farid, his best friend.
At the flat door he kicked his school bag so hard it skidded under the sofa. He slammed the bedroom door. When his older brother Suraj knocked to ask about evening cricket, Wasim yelled, "Go away! Nobody asked you!"
He sat on the bed, fists tight. Suraj hadn't laughed. Suraj hadn't done anything. But Ma'am was far away and too big to shout at, and at home yelling didn't cost anything.
Later, Ammi sat beside him. "Something happened at school?" Wasim stared at the floor, and then the whole story came out.

qa.q: What did Ma'am say when she held up Wasim's notebook?
qa.a: She said, "Is this handwriting or an ant walking in ink?"

qa.q: Why did yelling at Suraj feel okay to Wasim in that moment?
qa.a: Wasim was burning with embarrassment from class, but Ma'am was too big to shout at; home felt safe, so the anger came out there even though Suraj had done nothing.

qa.q: What turning point let the real story come out?
qa.a: Ammi sitting beside Wasim and asking about school rather than scolding the slammed door; that pointed straight at where the feeling came from.

qa.q: How might Suraj see the evening, left outside a slammed door?
qa.a: Suraj only wanted to ask about cricket, so the shout would feel hurtful and puzzling, as if Suraj had done something wrong without knowing what.

grounding: Shows a child humiliated by a teacher who kicks his bag, slams doors and yells at his brother at home, where the anger feels safe to spend.

"Arohi? You're back early—"
Bang. The bedroom door shook. Toffee pawed at the door where Arohi, eleven, had shut herself in.
"It's Kamal mama. Can I come in?"
"No!"
The door opened a crack. "Toffee, get LOST! You're so annoying!"
The dog backed away, ears flat.
"Okay," Kamal mama said. "I'll sit here on the floor. Toffee too."
Silence. Then: "Sir shouted at me in front of the whole relay team. I dropped the baton. He said I ruined it for everyone."
"In front of everyone. That's heavy."
"I'm not angry at Toffee."
"I know. Toffee might not know, though."
The door opened wider. Arohi knelt and rubbed the dog's ears. "Sorry, Toffee."
"Want to tell me the rest?"

qa.q: What happened at relay practice, according to Arohi?
qa.a: Arohi dropped the baton, and Sir shouted at her in front of the whole relay team.

qa.q: Why did Arohi snap at Toffee when her anger was really about Sir?
qa.a: Arohi felt humiliated 😢 and couldn't shout back at Sir, so the feeling spilled onto Toffee, who was close and safe; saying "I'm not angry at Toffee" shows she half knows it.

qa.q: Which choice by Kamal mama helped the story come out?
qa.a: Sitting on the floor outside the door and waiting, instead of pushing in or scolding the shout, gave Arohi room to say what really happened.

qa.q: What might Kamal mama be thinking when Arohi says, "I'm not angry at Toffee"?
qa.a: Kamal mama probably sees that Arohi already knows where the anger belongs, and gently points out that Toffee still felt it, so a small apology matters.

grounding: Illustrates a child humiliated at school practice who slams a door and snaps at the family dog at home, where the feeling is spent safely.
